alignment.note: All three open the verse with a coordinating conjunction plus the aorist/perfect verb of eating (ἔφαγον / ܐܟܠܘ / manducaverunt). Syriac fuses conjunction and verb into a single prefixed form ܘܐܟܠܘ, whereas Greek and Latin keep them as separate tokens.

The Greek postpositive particle δέ ('now, and') has no counterpart in either the Peshitta or the Vulgate, both of which render the narrative connective with simple conjunction only. The doubled καὶ … δέ is a Markan stylistic feature not reproduced in the versions.

Greek expresses 'and were satisfied' with conjunction plus passive aorist ἐχορτάσθησαν; Latin uses a periphrastic passive (saturati sunt) requiring two tokens plus its conjunction; Syriac again fuses conjunction and verb in ܘܣܒܥܘ (root s-b-e, cognate with Hebrew שׂבָע). Semantically identical, syntactically divergent.
The verb of gathering up the remnants (ἦραν / ܫܩܠܘ / sustulerunt) is preceded by a conjunction in all three; Syriac fuses the two as ܘܫܩܠܘ while Greek and Latin keep them discrete.

Greek has a compact noun phrase 'leftovers of fragments' (περισσεύματα κλασμάτων); Syriac mirrors this with construct-like ܬܘܬܪܐ ܕܩܨܝܐ ('remnants of pieces'). The Vulgate paraphrases with a relative clause, quod superaverat de fragmentis ('what had remained over of the fragments'), a syntactic expansion of the same idea rather than a literal rendering.

The Greek σπυρίδας (large rope baskets, distinct from the κόφινοι of the feeding of the five thousand) is rendered by the Syriac loan-word ܐܣܦܪܝܕܝܢ, itself a transliteration of the same Greek term, while the Latin sportas is the standard cognate Latin loan. All three preserve the lexical distinction proper to the second feeding miracle.
